The Mexican sheartail (Doricha eliza) is a diminutive hummingbird endemic to the Yucatán Peninsula, where it inhabits dry thorn forests and coastal scrub. Females construct a small cup nest using plant down and spider silk, typically laying two elliptical eggs that measure approximately 1.2 centimeters in length and 0.8 centimeters in width. From these dimensions, the calculated egg mass is about 0.4 grams, a value derived from the formula for an ellipsoid. At an incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the embryos develop rapidly and the eggs hatch after approximately 15 days [ab = approximately 15 days]. Upon emergence, the altricial nestlings exhibit a wet weight at birth of just 0.3 grams [Wwb = 0.3 grams], reflecting the extreme altriciality typical of trochilids. This meager neonatal mass places a substantial burden on the female, who must engage in frequent foraging bouts to provision the developing chicks with a diet of nectar and small arthropods throughout the early nestling phase.

Following hatching, the nestling period is characterized by a period of rapid mass gain, as the chicks transition from their initial mass to the much larger adult body size. Under the thermoneutral conditions typical of the species' active metabolic phase, measured at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], fledging occurs after approximately 23 days since birth [tx = approximately 23 days since birth]. This comparatively short time spent in the nest is consistent with the pattern observed in other small hummingbirds, where a high metabolic rate drives accelerated growth. The nestlings are brooded intensively for the first week, after which they begin to develop pin feathers and open their eyes. The fledgling period is a critical transition, as the young bird must achieve full thermoregulatory independence and the capability for sustained hovering flight to access floral nectar sources. Successful fledging marks the end of direct parental care, though the female may continue to provide supplemental feeds for a brief period as the juvenile refines its foraging skills.

The juvenile phase is followed by a period of gonadal maturation that, under the same active metabolic temperature regime of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], culminates in puberty at approximately 69 days since birth [tp = approximately 69 days since birth]. This rapid maturation, reaching sexual competence at just over two months of age, is among the fastest recorded for any hummingbird species of similar body size. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is approximately 3.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 3.5 grams], a mass that places Doricha eliza among the very smallest of the trochilids, comparable to the bee hummingbird. This diminutive adult size is associated with an extraordinarily high mass-specific metabolic rate. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from wild-caught individuals during the breeding season confirms that spermatogenesis and follicular development are well underway by this age, allowing the species to capitalize on brief peaks in floral resource abundance.

Reproductive timing in the Mexican sheartail is tightly linked to the onset of the rainy season, which triggers a flush of nectar-producing flowers. The first brood of the season is initiated approximately 365 days since birth [tR = approximately 365 days since birth], implying that most first-time breeders are in their second calendar year at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This delay, despite the earlier attainment of puberty, suggests that social factors or the energetic demands of establishing a territory may defer actual breeding. Females produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], a typical value for hummingbirds, and field observations indicate they raise approximately two clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately two clutches per year] during favorable conditions. The maximum reproduction rate is approximately 2 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 2 eggs per year]. The maximum recorded lifespan for this species is estimated at 10 years [am = 10 years], a longevity value derived from banding studies on the related black-chinned hummingbird (Archilochus alexandri) and assumed to be similar given the comparable metabolic constraints operating under a core temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C].

The energetic physiology of Doricha eliza is extreme, even by hummingbird standards, due to its minute body size. The daily reproductive output, calculated from a single egg per clutch and approximately two clutches annually, translates to a modest overall fecundity compared to other small endotherms, but it reflects a high per-capita investment in each offspring. Field studies on the Yucatán peninsula have documented that adult males defend small foraging territories, while females bear the full cost of nest construction, incubation, and provisioning. The combination of a fast life history—with a short developmental period and early maturation—and a small clutch size is typical of hummingbirds, where high adult survival and intense competition for nectar resources favor sustained reproductive effort over many years. This species thus exemplifies a strategy of iteroparity at a very small body size, balancing minimal per-event output against a potentially long adult lifespan of 10 years [am = 10 years], an achievement made possible by the extraordinarily efficient hovering flight and torpor capabilities that characterize the family Trochilidae at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C].
